title: 3 Fun Ways To Improve Your Observational Skills This Summer
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that good teachers succeed in part because they are keenly observant, and that observation is a skill that can be deliberately developed over the summer break. While strong classroom management provides the time and freedom to actually observe students, the underlying skill of noticing detail can be trained separately. He offers three daily exercises: taking one interesting photograph a day to train the eye for what stands out, taking in one scene a day through quiet, mindful sensory awareness, and sketching one remembered event or scene each night to sharpen recall. Each exercise is described in practical detail, including how and why it works. Linsin closes by urging teachers to try one of the exercises immediately, framing them as easy, soothing practices that ultimately make teachers more perceptive and more effective in the classroom.
points: Good classroom management creates the time and freedom needed to actually practice observation.
Taking one interesting photo per day trains teachers to notice detail and view the world through students' eyes.
A daily ten-minute sensory pause builds mindfulness and roots teachers in the present moment where good teaching happens.
Nightly sketching from memory sharpens recall and daily awareness, and incidentally improves storytelling ability.
The exercises are designed to pull teachers out of distraction and busyness so they can truly know their students.
quotes: Good teachers are observant. In fact, their students swear they have eyes in the back of their head.
Now, it’s important to mention that good classroom management is essential for becoming more observant.
This exercise helps you to notice details, to look for and appreciate what stands out from the rest—whether good, bad, or just plain different.
It trains you to view the world through an empathetic lens, to walk and teach while wearing your students’ shoes and seeing your instruction through their eyes.
Sweep away all conscious thought and tune into the moment using all of your senses.
Take a few minutes or more sometime before retiring to bed to sketch from memory one scene or event you witnessed that day.
Many, many teachers are so locked into a state of distraction, busyness, and micromanagement that they never really get to know their students.
